## Overview

In this episode, Jess hosts a prediction competition between Rich and guest James Reed (Professor of Economics at Reading University) to determine who will win the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The episode begins with an explanation of the new expanded 48-team tournament format, including the complex rules for determining the eight best third-place teams from 495 possible combinations. Rich explains his ELO-based methodology for calculating match outcomes, including a novel approach to incorporating draw probabilities using historical data from Betfair.

## Key Concepts

::: {.callout-tip}
## ELO Ratings for Match Prediction
ELO ratings provide a numerical measure of team strength that can be used to calculate win probabilities. Rich took ratings from eloratings.net and used the standard ELO formula to determine the probability of each team winning, acknowledging limitations due to teams not playing each other frequently (e.g., Uruguay rarely plays Germany).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Adjusting for Draws in Football
Unlike basketball, football matches can end in draws, which standard ELO doesn't account for. Rich's solution was to calculate the difference in win probabilities between teams, then look up historical data showing how often matches with that probability difference ended in draws, rescaling the win/loss probabilities accordingly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Monte Carlo Tournament Simulation
To predict tournament outcomes, Rich ran 10,000 iterations of the entire World Cup, randomly selecting match winners based on calculated probabilities at each stage. This approach builds out the full tournament bracket repeatedly to estimate each team's chances of winning.
:::

## Transcript Highlights

> "There are 495 mathematical combinations for the eighth best third place teams. And every potential outcome is indeed listed in Annex C pages 80 to 97 of the 2026 FIFA World Cup regulations."

Jess highlights the remarkable complexity of the new World Cup format, where FIFA had to enumerate every possible combination of qualifying third-place teams to ensure bracket integrity.

---

> "England would have around a 76% chance of winning... around 16% chance of a draw and around 7% chance of a Scotland win."

Rich demonstrates his model with a concrete example of England vs Scotland at Wembley, showing how ELO ratings translate into specific match probabilities.

---

> "I didn't realize we were fully competing. I thought... yeah, now I'm nervous."

James Reed's reaction upon learning his predictions would be directly compared to Rich's, capturing the friendly competitive spirit of the episode.

## Discussion

This episode showcases the practical challenges of applying mathematical models to real-world sporting events. The 2026 World Cup's expanded format introduces significant complexity that modellers must navigate, from the 495 possible third-place combinations to the intricate tiebreaker rules that go beyond simple goal difference. Rich's approach of using historical draw data to augment ELO ratings demonstrates how practitioners often need to combine multiple data sources to address limitations in standard methods.

The competition format between Rich and James highlights an important aspect of sports analytics: different reasonable methodologies can lead to different predictions. By having two experts tackle the same problem independently, the episode implicitly explores model uncertainty and the value of comparing approaches. This connects to broader themes in forecasting and prediction markets, where aggregating multiple models often outperforms any single approach.
